terms.definition: A short, specific stretch of DNA that carries the instructions to build one protein, or to influence one trait.
terms.function: Stores the instructions a cell reads to build one particular protein.
terms.whereItIs: Found at a specific spot, called a locus, along a chromosome.
terms.whyItMatters: Genes are the reason children resemble their parents and the reason some illnesses run in families — they're the instruction manual for every living thing.

terms.definition: The short, defined stretch of the DNA double helix that makes up one whole gene, from the start of its promoter to the end of its coding sequence.
terms.function: Physically holds one gene's full instruction set within the much longer DNA molecule that makes up a chromosome.
terms.whereItIs: The brighter, full-opacity band of the helix, standing out from the dimmed context strand that fades away above and below it.
terms.whyItMatters: Recognizing a gene as one bounded stretch within a much longer strand is the foundation for understanding that a chromosome carries thousands of separate genes, not just one continuous instruction.

terms.definition: A short DNA sequence right before a gene's coding sequence that acts like an 'on switch,' telling the cell where to start reading that gene.
terms.function: Signals to the cell's copying machinery where a particular gene begins, so reading starts in the right place.
terms.whereItIs: The short amber-gold band at the upstream (start) end of the highlighted gene segment.
terms.whyItMatters: If a promoter is damaged, the gene that follows it may never get read at all, even if the coding sequence itself is perfectly intact.

terms.definition: The part of a gene that spells out, letter by letter, the instructions for building a protein.
terms.function: Provides the actual template the cell reads to assemble a specific protein, one building block at a time.
terms.whereItIs: The longer teal-blue band that immediately follows the promoter region within the highlighted gene segment.
terms.whyItMatters: This is where the gene's real information lives — changes (mutations) here can change the protein that gets built, and sometimes the trait it produces.

terms.definition: The single protein a gene's coding sequence is used to build, which can in turn shape one observable trait.
terms.function: Represents the end result of reading a gene — a working protein molecule that goes on to do a job in the body.
terms.whereItIs: The small folded-ribbon shape floating just past the end of the coding sequence, connected to it by a thin leader line.
terms.whyItMatters: A gene doesn't produce a trait directly — it produces a protein first, and it's that protein's action that shapes the trait we can actually observe.

terms.definition: The long, twisted molecule (shaped like a spiral ladder) that stores genetic instructions using four chemical letters: A, T, C, and G.
terms.function: Serves as the physical storage medium for every gene an organism has.
terms.whereItIs: Coiled up inside the nucleus of almost every cell in the body, packaged into chromosomes.
terms.whyItMatters: DNA is the shared molecule every gene is made of — understanding its structure is the basis for understanding how genes work.

terms.definition: A tightly coiled, thread-like package of DNA. Genes are arranged along chromosomes like beads on a string.
terms.function: Organizes and protects an organism's DNA, keeping many genes bundled together in an orderly, copyable form.
terms.whereItIs: Packed inside the nucleus of a cell; humans typically have 23 pairs.
terms.whyItMatters: A chromosome is the larger structure a gene 'belongs to' — this is the level a gene sits inside of before you zoom out to the whole cell.

terms.definition: The specific address, or location, where a gene sits on a chromosome.
terms.function: Gives every gene a fixed, identifiable position, so the same gene is found at the same spot on the same chromosome in every individual of a species.
terms.whereItIs: A specific point along a chromosome's length.
terms.whyItMatters: Because a gene's locus is fixed, scientists and doctors can reliably find and study the same gene across different people.

terms.definition: One specific version of a gene. Different people can carry different alleles of the same gene, which is why the same gene can produce different outcomes.
terms.function: Accounts for variation between individuals — since everyone has the same genes but not always the same alleles of them.
terms.whereItIs: At the same locus as the gene it's a version of; a person typically carries two alleles of most genes, one inherited from each parent.
terms.whyItMatters: A gene and an allele are not the same thing: everyone carries the ABO blood-type gene, for example, but which alleles (A, B, or O) they carry determines their actual blood type.

terms.definition: An observable characteristic — like blood type or the ability to taste a certain bitter chemical — that a gene (sometimes combined with the environment) helps produce.
terms.function: Represents the visible or measurable outcome that results, often indirectly, from a gene's protein product.
terms.whereItIs: Not a physical structure itself — it's an observable result of proteins doing their work throughout the body.
terms.whyItMatters: Traits are how genetics becomes visible in everyday life — they're the reason siblings can share features, and the reason some conditions run in families.
